input:
In this example we look at a vapour-compression refrigeration unit that serves an ice rink, and we compare the performance it actually achieves with the best performance that could in principle be achieved between the same temperatures. The unit operates with an evaporating temperature of -25 °C and a condensing temperature of 35 °C. Between these two temperatures, the Carnot coefficient of performance works out to 4.13, whereas the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.03, so there is a considerable gap between the two figures.

The coefficient of performance, or COP, is essentially a measure of how much cooling effect is obtained for each unit of work that is supplied to the machine. The Carnot COP represents the theoretical upper limit for any refrigerator that works between a given pair of temperatures, which in this case are -25 °C on the cold side and 35 °C on the hot side, and no real machine can do better than this limit of 4.13. The installed unit's figure of 2.03 corresponds to about 0.49 of the Carnot value, which gives a simple way of expressing how close the real machine comes to the ideal.

It is important to bear in mind, however, that the achieved figure comes from the manufacturer's own test, carried out at full load. The performance of the unit at part load is not stated anywhere, and in practice an ice rink does not call for full-load operation all of the time. The comparison that has been made is therefore strictly a full-load comparison, and it should not be taken as a description of how the unit behaves across the whole range of loads that the rink places on it over a season.
target:
The installed vapour-compression unit at the ice rink achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.03, against a Carnot coefficient of performance of 4.13 between the same two temperatures. The unit evaporates at -25 °C and condenses at 35 °C, and the achieved figure is the manufacturer's test value at full load.

The coefficient of performance states the cooling duty delivered per unit of work supplied. The Carnot value is the ceiling for any refrigerator working between the two temperatures: no machine between an evaporating temperature of -25 °C and a condensing temperature of 35 °C exceeds 4.13, and a real machine stands below the ceiling by the losses its cycle carries. The installed unit, at 2.03, delivers 0.49 of the Carnot performance. The two coefficients share the same temperatures, and the comparison holds the duty fixed. That ratio is the finding of the comparison; it is computed from the two stated coefficients and from nothing else. The distance between the two values is the room the cycle leaves for improvement, and it is read against the ceiling rather than against another machine, because no second machine is stated.

What the figure does not state is how the unit performs away from the test point. The achieved value comes from the manufacturer's test at full load, and part-load performance is not stated. A season at an ice rink is not run at full load throughout, and the rink's energy use follows the part-load behaviour that the test figure leaves open. The comparison is therefore a full-load comparison. It ranks the installed unit against the ceiling for its duty, and it says nothing about the unit's standing across the load range the rink actually imposes. A part-load figure would be needed before the unit's seasonal performance can be stated.
